title: 1 Samuel 3:11–18
context: The LORD tells Samuel that he will carry out all he has spoken against Eli’s house, because Eli knew of his sons’ sin and did not restrain them, and that the iniquity of Eli’s house will not be removed by sacrifice or offering. In the morning Samuel fears to tell Eli, but at Eli’s insistence he tells him everything, and Eli replies, “It is the LORD. Let him do what seems good to him.” Both traditions read this soberly as God’s just judgment on persistent priestly corruption and shared ground on God’s holiness.

verses.text: The LORD said to Samuel, “Behold, I will do a thing in Israel at which both the ears of everyone who hears it will tingle.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says he will do something in Israel that will make the ears of all who hear tingle. Arminian readers note the shock of what is coming (cf. 2 Kings 21:12; Jer 19:3).

The first message to the young prophet is one of judgment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see the gravity of what God announces.

God’s first word to Samuel shows that a prophet must speak hard truth as well as comfort.

verses.text: In that day I will perform against Eli all that I have spoken concerning his house, from the beginning even to the end.
verses.arminianNotes:
God will perform all he spoke against Eli’s house, from beginning to end. Arminian readers note that this confirms the earlier warning by the man of God (1 Sam 2:27–36).

God’s word of judgment, like his word of promise, will be fulfilled.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness to his word in judgment.

The repetition of the earlier message shows that it was not an empty threat.

verses.text: For I have told him that I will judge his house forever for the iniquity which he knew, because his sons brought a curse on themselves, and he didn’t restrain them.
verses.arminianNotes:
God will judge Eli’s house for the iniquity he knew, because his sons brought a curse on themselves and he did not restrain them. Arminian readers stress Eli’s responsibility as father and priest: he knew and failed to act.

The sons’ sins are described in chapter 2 (2:12–17, 22–25).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see Eli’s culpable failure to discipline his sons and the seriousness of corrupting God’s worship.

Both traditions read the judgment as just, falling on a priestly house that persisted in known sin.

verses.text: Therefore I have sworn to the house of Eli that the iniquity of Eli’s house shall not be removed with sacrifice or offering forever.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The iniquity of Eli’s house will not be removed by sacrifice or offering forever. Arminian readers often read this in light of persistent, high-handed sin for which the sacrificial system made no provision (cf. Num 15:30–31).

The verdict concerns the priestly house’s standing, not a statement about every individual’s eternal state.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see judgment on defiant sin within the priesthood (cf. Heb 10:26).

The removal of Eli’s line from the high priesthood is later recorded (1 Kings 2:27). Both traditions treat the oath as a sober judgment on a house, without speculating about individuals’ final destiny.

verses.text: Samuel lay until the morning, and opened the doors of the LORD’s house. Samuel was afraid to show Eli the vision.
verses.arminianNotes:
Samuel lies until morning, opens the doors of the LORD’s house, and is afraid to tell Eli. Arminian readers note his human hesitation and his continued routine duties.

Receiving God’s word does not remove the difficulty of delivering it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the young prophet’s natural fear and his faithfulness in ordinary service.

The tension prepares for the test of whether he will speak the whole truth.

verses.text: Then Eli called Samuel and said, “Samuel, my son!” He said, “Here I am.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Eli calls, “Samuel, my son!” and Samuel answers, “Here I am.” Arminian readers note the tender address and Samuel’s respectful response.

The relationship between the old priest and the boy remains warm.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the same words Samuel used to God now spoken to Eli.

Samuel’s readiness extends to his human superior, even when the message is painful.

verses.text: He said, “What is the thing that he has spoken to you? Please don’t hide it from me. God do so to you, and more also, if you hide anything from me of all the things that he spoke to you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Eli presses Samuel not to hide anything, with a solemn oath. Arminian readers note that Eli wants the truth even if it is hard.

His insistence suggests he suspects what the message is.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see Eli seeking God’s word despite fearing it.

The oath formula underlines the seriousness of withholding God’s message.

verses.text: Samuel told him every bit, and hid nothing from him. He said, “It is the LORD. Let him do what seems good to him.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Samuel tells everything, and Eli says, “It is the LORD. Let him do what seems good to him.” Arminian readers note Eli’s acceptance, though some see resignation rather than repentance.

Interpreters differ on whether Eli’s reply is faith or passivity.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers often hear submission to God’s sovereign will (cf. Job 1:21; 2:10), while noting that Eli does not change his sons’ conduct.

Both traditions see Samuel’s full honesty as a mark of a true prophet.
